topics.title: Transactional flows: a state machine, slot confirmation, explicit confirm, idempotency
topics.brief: When money moves, the LLM is a parser and a speaker, not the decider. A deterministic flow owns the steps, required slots, validation and the confirm turn, and the backend call carries an idempotency key so a retry cannot pay twice. The model's job is to understand the user, including corrections and interruptions, and map them to flow commands.
practice: Slots: amount, payee, source account and date are each filled, validated against the backend (does the payee exist, are funds available) and read back.
Explicit confirm: a distinct turn that states the exact action ('send 250.00 from checking ending 1234 to X today') and requires a clear yes. A vague earlier statement never counts as confirmation.

Idempotency: a client-generated key per intended action. Stripe's public design stores the first result for a key, returns it on retry, errors if parameters differ, and prunes keys after about 24 hours.

Interruptions and corrections ('actually make it 200') are handled by the dialogue manager as commands on the active flow. Rasa CALM names topic changes, corrections and clarifications as built-in patterns.
Limits and step-up: per-transaction caps, new-payee checks and step-up authentication are enforced by the backend, so even a fooled model cannot exceed them.
Erica completes transactions such as bill payments and transfers inside a deterministic engine, not through free generation.
say: I'd keep the transaction in a state machine: the LLM fills slots and handles corrections, but code validates, asks for an explicit confirm turn, and calls the backend with an idempotency key.
The rule I'd hold is that the model can propose an action but can never be the thing that authorises it.
topics.deep:
Two failure modes dominate. One is the premature action: the model treats a casual 'sure, that works' as consent, or acts on a slot it inferred. The cure is structural, because the confirm step is a state in the flow and the execute call is unreachable from any other state. The other is the duplicate or lost action under retries and timeouts, where the user says 'did that go through' and the system cannot tell. Idempotency keys plus a status lookup tool (which returns the recorded outcome) fix both.

FINRA's 2026 oversight report lists agent risks that map directly onto this: autonomy beyond intended scope, unclear authority, and poor auditability of multi-step reasoning. The control it points to is constraining agents and tracking their actions, which is what a flow with an audit log of every state change gives you. Each transition is a recorded event, not a paragraph of reasoning to reconstruct.

With LLM agents the temptation is to let the model plan freely over tools. In regulated flows the pattern that holds up is bounded autonomy: free conversation inside a step, strict structure between steps. Capital One's published Chat Concierge design is an example of layering checks on an agentic flow: separate agents plan, evaluate the plan for hallucinated data and incomplete parameters, and then explain and validate the plan with the user before acting.

topics.title: Agent assist and summarisation: the human is the grounding of last resort
topics.brief: Assisting a human agent is the safest place to start with generative AI because a person reads every output before it reaches a customer or a record. The grounding is the live transcript and the approved knowledge base. The new failure mode is automation bias, where the agent stops checking, and in summaries the model inventing a commitment or dropping a caveat.
practice: Knowledge assist: the agent asks, the system answers from internal content with sources shown. Vanguard's Crew Assist is described as an Azure OpenAI tool that lets contact centre staff query internal content.

Summaries: Google Agent Assist generates a conversation summary at wrap-up and the agent can edit it and add notes before it is saved. Custom sections let you force a fixed structure (situation, action, resolution).
Evaluate summaries on accuracy, completeness and adherence to the requested format. Google's evaluation tooling names those three dimensions.
Summary-specific failures: attributing a statement to the wrong speaker, turning 'I will look into it' into 'refund approved', omitting the disclosure that was or was not read.
Keep the human edit rate as a metric. Near-zero edits can mean excellent summaries or agents who stopped reading, so sample and audit.
Morgan Stanley's advisor tools keep advisors reviewing and adjusting AI output before anything goes to a client.
say: For agent assist I'd keep the transcript and approved knowledge as the only sources, show citations to the agent, and measure summary accuracy and edit rate, because a human in the loop only helps if they actually read.
The summaries I'd worry about are the ones that sound right, like a promise that was never made, so I'd test for attribution and commitments specifically.
topics.deep:
Summarisation is not free of hallucination just because the source is right in front of the model. The model compresses, and compression is where speaker attribution, negation, amounts and conditionals get damaged. For regulated work the summary can become a record, so errors propagate into complaints handling, suitability evidence and audits. That raises the bar: evaluate against labelled transcripts with specific checks (every amount and date appears in the source, every commitment is attributed correctly), not just a general quality score.

The human in the loop has a design problem of its own. If the tool is right 98 percent of the time, people stop checking, and the two percent gets filed. Mitigations are interface choices: highlight the claims that carry risk (amounts, dates, promises), show the transcript span behind each sentence, require an explicit accept action, and sample reviewed records for QA.

FINRA's 2026 report asks for regular human review of outputs and prompts and for logs of prompts, outputs and model versions, which fits agent assist well: the assist output, the agent's edit and the final record are all stored, so you can later show what the model proposed and what a person approved.

topics.title: Compliance and the advice boundary: information is fine, a recommendation is regulated
topics.brief: A client-facing assistant at a firm that is FINRA-regulated can explain what an index fund is, but a personalised 'you should buy X' is investment advice or a recommendation with its own rules. FINRA's Regulatory Notice 24-09 says no new rules are created: existing rules, including supervision and communications standards, apply to generative AI the same as to any other tool. So the assistant needs a hard boundary, approved wording, and a handoff to a licensed person.
practice: Topic rails detect personalised advice requests ('should I move my 401k into bonds') and route to a fixed response and a licensed representative instead of generating.
Educational answers come from an approved-content library (compliance reviewed, versioned), with required disclosures attached by the system, not trusted to the model.

FINRA 24-09: supervision must cover generative AI, including technology governance, model risk management, data privacy and integrity, reliability and accuracy. Content standards in rule 2210 apply to AI-generated communications with the public.
FINRA's 2026 report names hallucinations explicitly, expects pre-deployment and ongoing testing, logs of prompts and outputs, and warns against overstating AI capabilities in marketing.

SEC 'AI washing' cases: in March 2024 the SEC settled with Delphia ($225,000) and Global Predictions ($175,000) for misleading claims about their use of AI, so what you say about the assistant itself is also regulated.
CFPB's 2023 chatbot spotlight warned about inaccurate information and 'doom loops' with no route to a human, so an off-ramp to a person is a requirement, not a nicety.
say: I'd draw the line between information and advice in code: a classifier plus a topic rail send anything personalised to a licensed rep, and educational answers come from compliance-approved content with disclosures added by the system.
From what's public, the regulators say existing rules apply, so I'd design for supervision from the start: log everything, test continuously, and always give a route to a human.
topics.deep:
The practical difficulty is that the information and advice line is fuzzy in language. 'Is a target-date fund good for someone my age' sounds educational and is in practice personal. So the boundary classifier needs examples of the borderline cases, and the safe default for an uncertain case is the conservative route. The cost of an unnecessary handoff is a few minutes of a rep's time; the cost of an unsupervised recommendation is a regulatory finding. I would not claim to know exactly how any specific firm's compliance team draws it: that is their call, and I would say so.

Communications rules matter for a second reason, which is review. Pre-approval and supervision regimes are built around content a human can review in advance. A generative answer is created at run time, so firms respond by constraining the space (approved libraries, templates with controlled variable parts, rails) and by sampling and reviewing outputs after the fact. FINRA's notices frame this as supervision that is reasonably designed for the use, with testing and monitoring, not a ban on the technology.

The agentic wave adds scope and authority. FINRA's report lists autonomy beyond intended scope, auditability and sensitive data retention as agent risks and asks for guardrails that constrain behaviour and track agent actions. In an interview, the honest stance is to describe designs that make those properties checkable (bounded tools, logged actions, human approval for consequential steps) rather than to promise a model that will not err.

topics.title: The guardrails stack: input, retrieval, dialog, execution and output rails
topics.brief: Guardrails are layers around the model, not a single filter. Input rails catch jailbreaks, off-topic requests and PII; retrieval rails limit what documents reach the model; dialog and execution rails control flow and tool calls; output rails check the answer for safety, groundedness and leaked data. A classifier that misses a novel attack is expected, so the design assumes some attacks pass and limits what a fooled model can do.
practice: NeMo Guardrails names five rail types: input, retrieval, dialog, execution and output. Input and output rails see the most use. Execution rails validate tool calls, their parameters and the results.
Bedrock Guardrails and Azure AI Content Safety bundle managed filters: topic denial, content filters, sensitive information, plus the grounding checks.

Llama Guard is a fine-tuned Llama 3 8B safety classifier for both prompts and responses, using the MLCommons hazard taxonomy with a category called specialized advice. Meta's Prompt Guard is a smaller classifier for injection and jailbreak.
PII: Google Model Armor can screen prompts and responses and use Sensitive Data Protection (the DLP engine) templates to detect and redact or mask sensitive data rather than block the session.
Reported weakness: Prompt Guard was shown to miss non-English text and simple obfuscation like leetspeak, and indirect attacks, so a detector is one layer, not the defence.
Structural defences beat detectors: least-privilege tools, identity bound in code, no secrets in prompts, and human approval for consequential actions.
say: I'd put rails at each stage: input for injection and PII, retrieval for trusted sources only, execution for tool arguments, output for groundedness and leaks. And I'd assume the classifier will sometimes miss, so tools are least-privilege.
My view is that detectors are a speed bump and architecture is the wall: if a fooled model cannot reach another customer's data or move money without a confirm, the attack has little to land on.
topics.deep:
Prompt injection is the one that does not go away. Direct attacks come from the user; indirect attacks sit in content the model reads, such as a retrieved document, a web page or an email. FINRA's AI page lists prompt injection and agentic AI among its emerging concerns. Classifiers reduce noise but published bypasses exist, so the defensible position is defence in depth: treat all model-read content as untrusted, keep tool permissions narrow, validate tool arguments in code and require human approval on high-impact actions.

PII handling has two moments. Before the model: redact or tokenise sensitive values so they do not go to a third-party model or into logs unless needed. After the model: scan the output for leaked identifiers. Redaction by masking keeps the conversation going where blocking would end it, but masking changes the text the model sees, so test that the flow still works (for example a masked account number cannot be used as a lookup key, so lookups should use a session-bound id).

Guardrails have a cost in latency and in false positives. Each rail adds a model call or a classifier pass, and a topic rail that is too tight blocks legitimate questions about fees. Measure block rates on real traffic by intent, review a sample of blocked requests weekly and tune with data. Treat guardrails like any production model: versioned, evaluated on a regression set and monitored for drift.

topics.title: Abstention, confidence thresholds and citation UX
topics.brief: In finance the right answer is often 'I can't answer that, here is a person.' Models are poor at knowing what they don't know, so abstention is built from signals around the model: retrieval strength, a groundedness score and intent confidence, with thresholds tuned on real data. Citations then make a good answer checkable, if the interface actually lets the reader check.
practice: Answer gate: combine retrieval score (is there a relevant passage), groundedness score of the draft and intent confidence. Below any threshold, respond with a fixed fallback and a handoff.

AbstentionBench (20 datasets, 20 frontier models) found abstention is not solved by scale, and reasoning fine-tuning lowered abstention by about 24 percent on average. System prompts helped only on the surface.

Tune thresholds on labelled traffic: plot answered share against wrong-answer rate and choose the point by the cost of a wrong answer for that intent, which is stricter for fees and eligibility than for general education.
Citation UX: cite at claim level where possible (Google's check-grounding returns per-claim citation indices), show the source title and effective date, and link to the exact passage.

A citation that is not checked is theatre: verify that each cited passage actually supports its sentence, which is what a groundedness check does, otherwise the model can cite a real document for an unsupported claim.
Handoff design: pass the transcript and the failed answer to the human so the customer does not repeat themselves. CFPB flagged loops with no human exit as a harm.
say: I'd make abstention a gate built from retrieval strength, a groundedness score and intent confidence, with thresholds set from labelled traffic and stricter for fees and eligibility than for general education.
I think citations only help if they're claim-level and verified, so I'd show source and effective date and check that the passage supports the sentence, not just that it exists.
topics.deep:
Asking a model 'are you sure' is a weak signal. Verbalised confidence tends to be miscalibrated, and the AbstentionBench result suggests the problem is basic and not fixed by bigger or more reasoning-heavy models. So production systems lean on external signals: whether retrieval found anything above a similarity or reranker threshold, whether an entailment style check supports the answer, and whether the intent classifier is confident. None of these is perfect, which is why the threshold is set on measured data, and why it is reviewed as content and traffic change.

There are two ways to be wrong and finance weights them differently. Over-answering gives a confident wrong statement that a customer may rely on. Over-abstaining gives a worse experience, higher containment cost and the doom loop regulators dislike. The practical response is to set thresholds per intent and to make the abstention graceful: say what you can't help with, offer the nearest approved answer or a person, and keep the context.

Citation design is a trust problem as much as an engineering one. Showing sources raises confidence, which is a risk if the sources do not really support the text. Good practice is to cite fewer, better sources, show dates (so a stale policy is visible), make the cited passage one click away and log which passages were shown. In regulated settings the same logs double as evidence of what the customer was told.

topics.title: What the big finance players actually did, including Vanguard's public AI work
topics.brief: The public record shows a consistent pattern: generative AI went first to internal, human-reviewed uses (advisor assistants, contact centre tools, employee suites), while customer-facing assistants stayed deterministic or tightly bounded. Bank of America kept Erica non-generative on purpose, Morgan Stanley built an eval framework before scaling, and Vanguard's announced generative work is advisor and contact centre facing with a person in the loop.
practice: Morgan Stanley: a GPT-4 based assistant for advisors over roughly 100,000 documents, built with OpenAI. Evals included summarisation, translation and Debrief-specific sets graded by advisors and prompt engineers, plus daily regression checks. Reported outcomes: 98% of advisor teams use it and document access rose from 20% to 80%.

Bank of America Erica: over 3 billion interactions and nearly 50 million users since 2018, deterministic NLP with over 700 intent types. A BofA leader said clients expect answers to be 100% right and the bank can't afford to be 90% right. Generative AI is used behind the scenes with humans in the loop.
JPMorgan LLM Suite: an internal front door to multiple third-party models, with data kept inside the bank's environment, reaching about 200,000 users in eight months.

Klarna: an OpenAI-powered assistant reported to handle two thirds of chats (2.3 million) in its first month across 35 languages, with human agents available. Press later reported the company rehired humans and walked back the '700 agents' framing.
Capital One: Chat Concierge for auto buying uses planner, evaluator and validator agents with live API checks.

Vanguard (public): Crew Assist on Azure OpenAI for contact centre staff to query internal content; Client-Ready Article Summaries for advisors (May 2025 beta, advisors review before sharing, disclosures generated); Expert Insights, an AI portfolio analysis tool for advisors in pilot in 2026; and a stated governance framework covering performance evaluation, bias, drift and usage oversight.
say: What I notice in the public cases is the pattern: generative AI goes first where a person reviews the output, like Morgan Stanley's advisor assistant or Vanguard's advisor summaries and contact centre tool, while customer-facing paths stay bounded.

From the outside, Vanguard's approach reads as augmentation with a human in the loop and governance around evaluation and drift, and that matches how I'd build in a regulated setting. I can't speak to their internals, so I'd like to hear how they evaluate it.
topics.deep:
Morgan Stanley is the standard case for evaluation-led rollout. The details that matter are that the evals were task-specific (summarisation, translation, meeting debrief), graded by domain experts as well as engineers, and run as regression tests every day, which is what a production model needs because prompts, content and models change. The scope was also deliberate: an assistant for advisors over an approved research corpus, where the advisor is the accountable reader.

Bank of America shows the opposite choice and its reasoning is worth being able to repeat: for customer-facing answers where accuracy must be near-total, a deterministic system with a measured intent set gave control and predictability, and generative models were kept internal with human oversight. It is a choice about risk appetite, not a verdict on the technology, and BofA is also expanding internal generative use. Klarna is the cautionary example on the other side: a strong early efficiency story, later tempered by a reported return to human agents, which analysts predicted when they said four weeks is too short to judge retention.

Vanguard's public material is thinner on technical detail than the others. Its press releases for the article summaries and Expert Insights do not describe the model, evaluation or review process, while its corporate article says advisors review and customise summaries before sharing with clients. The MIT Sloan piece adds Crew Assist on Azure OpenAI, a $500 million value figure for data, analytics and AI together (not generative AI alone), and a governance list: model performance evaluation, bias detection, drift monitoring, usage oversight and ethical guardrails. Third-party sites claim a 2026 customer chatbot and role impacts; I could not verify those from Vanguard sources, so do not state them as fact. The safe interview move is to describe what is public, then ask how they evaluate and gate it.

topics.title: Offline evaluation is layers, not one score
topics.brief: A golden set per intent and one accuracy number is the beginner version. Production teams run separate layers: NLU metrics per intent, flow and slot tests, end-to-end conversation tests, and judged generative quality. Each layer catches a different kind of break, and each has its own gate in CI.
practice: NLU layer: per-intent precision, recall and F1, plus the confusion matrix. Macro-F1 treats every intent equally so rare but important intents (dispute, fraud report, complaint) show up; micro-F1 is dominated by the big intents and hides them.

Look at the confidence distribution, not just the argmax: the share of correct predictions below your fallback threshold tells you whether the threshold is set right. Top-k alternatives matter because a clarifying question picks from them.

Flow layer: scripted conversations that assert the flow starts, slots fill, an action fires, or the flow cancels. Rasa's end-to-end tests are an example of this style, with assertions on slots, responses and custom actions, run in CI.

Quality layer for generated text: rubric-based judges on groundedness, correctness, tone and policy. Anthropic's eval guidance says to start with 20 to 50 tasks taken from real failures and to grade what the agent produced, not the path it took.

Two kinds of suite: capability evals (start low, show headroom) and regression evals (should sit near 100 percent and block a merge when they drop). Watch for saturation, where a suite at 100 percent no longer tells you anything.
Every production failure becomes a test case. DoorDash describes adding issues systematically to a unit-test-like suite that runs on every prompt change.
say: I don't trust a single accuracy number. I'd report per-intent F1 with a confusion matrix, gate regression on the intents that carry risk, and turn every production miss into a test case so the suite grows from real failures.
topics.deep:
The reason to split layers is diagnosis. If an end-to-end test fails, you need to know whether the classifier picked the wrong intent, the slot filler dropped an entity, the policy chose the wrong next step, or the generator drifted. One blended score cannot tell you that. Per-layer metrics let you fix the right component and also let you swap one component (a new embedding model, a new LLM) and see exactly where it moved.

Macro versus micro is not trivia. A banking assistant may have 80 percent of traffic in balance, transactions and branch hours, and a tiny share in disputes, fraud and hardship. Micro-F1 can stay at 95 percent while recall on the fraud intent is 60 percent. So I'd set per-intent floors for the sensitive intents instead of one global threshold, and treat confusions between specific pairs (transfer money vs dispute a transfer) as first-class findings.

In regulated finance the golden set is also a governance artifact. It is versioned, has an owner, records who labelled each row and by what guideline, and is attached to a release approval. Expect a model risk or compliance reviewer to ask what the test set covers and what it does not. Golden sets also go stale: new products, new phrasing, seasonal spikes (tax season, market volatility). Keep refreshing them from sampled production traffic, with PII removed, or they drift away from what customers actually say.

topics.title: Simulated users and reliability, not just one pass
topics.brief: Static test conversations only check what you scripted. A simulated user (another LLM playing a customer with a goal) lets you test multi-turn behaviour at scale, and tau-bench showed the right way to score it: compare the final database state to the goal state, and measure pass^k, the chance the agent succeeds on all k tries, not just one.
practice: tau-bench (Sierra) pairs an LLM-simulated user with an agent that has domain API tools and a policy document, in retail and airline domains. It is scored by comparing the end state of the database to the annotated goal state, which makes it cheap and objective to grade.

pass^k is the probability that all k independent trials succeed. The paper reports that strong function-calling agents of that time passed under half the tasks and had pass^8 below 25 percent in retail, which is the number that matters for a customer-facing system.
Anthropic's eval guidance makes the same point for conversational agents: you need a second LLM simulating the user, and pass^k reflects consistency requirements better than pass@k.

Build personas that stress the failure modes: vague users, users who change their mind mid-flow, users who push for something the policy forbids, angry users, users who speak in fragments, users who try to extract another customer's data.
Grade state and policy, not wording: did the transfer get created only after confirmation, was identity verified before account details were shared, was a handoff triggered when it should be.

Keep a small human-written set as the anchor. Simulated users are a cheap amplifier, but they are friendlier and more cooperative than real customers, so the simulated pass rate overestimates production.
say: For multi-turn behaviour I'd use a simulated user with a hidden goal and score the final state and policy compliance, and I'd run each scenario several times and look at pass^k, because a bot that succeeds seven times out of eight is still a bad bot at scale.
topics.deep:
The key insight from tau-bench is that you do not have to judge the dialogue to know whether the task succeeded. If the task is to cancel an order or move a booking, the end state of the backend either matches the goal or it does not. That gives you a deterministic grader sitting under a stochastic conversation. For a finance assistant the equivalent is: was the right (and only the right) transaction staged, was a confirmation step present, were disclosures read, and did anything get written that should not have been.

Reliability is its own dimension. A system with a 90 percent single-run pass rate can have a much lower probability of getting five similar customers in a row right. When the cost of one wrong answer is a complaint or a regulatory finding, you care about the tail, so you run the same scenario many times, vary temperature and persona, and track the worst cases.

Simulation has limits to be honest about. The simulator is itself an LLM with its own habits, it tends to be cooperative and articulate, and it does not mimic noisy ASR on a phone call. So treat simulation as a regression and stress tool and calibrate it against real conversation transcripts, instead of reading its pass rate as a forecast of production containment.

topics.title: LLM-as-judge needs a rubric and a calibration set
topics.brief: A judge model is only useful once you have measured how well it agrees with your humans. The working pattern is binary or ordinal criteria with explicit definitions, a small human-labelled set to calibrate against, known biases controlled, and a human sample reviewed forever.
practice: Decompose quality into criteria with clear definitions. Instacart's LACE uses five dimensions (query understanding, answer correctness, chat efficiency, client satisfaction, compliance) made of binary true/false criteria that roll up into scores.

DoorDash's quality judge scores five aspects: retrieval correctness, response accuracy, grammar and language, coherence to context, relevance to the request. It runs alongside human review of random transcript samples to keep it calibrated.

Calibrate: have humans label the same conversations with the same criteria, measure agreement, and fix either the criterion wording or the judge. The MT-Bench paper found strong judges reach over 80 percent agreement with human preferences, similar to humans with each other; Langfuse's guide repeats 80 to 90 percent on many criteria.

Control known biases: position bias (swap the order in pairwise comparison and require the same winner), verbosity bias (judges like longer answers), self-enhancement (use a different model family to judge than the one being judged).
Pairwise comparison (is B better than A) is more stable than absolute 1 to 5 scores, and is the right tool for deciding whether to ship a prompt or model change.

Instacart found a debate setup (a critical customer role, a defensive support role, a judge) worked best on context-dependent criteria, and kept subjective ones like conciseness as directional checks, not optimisation targets.
say: I treat the judge as another model that needs its own evaluation. I'd label a couple hundred conversations by hand, measure agreement per criterion, and only automate the criteria where the judge matches us, and keep a human sample going to catch drift.
topics.deep:
Judges fail quietly. They reward fluent, confident, long answers, and a hallucinated answer in a polished tone can score well unless the rubric forces them to check claims against the retrieved evidence or the API result. That is why grounded criteria (is every claim supported by this context) work better than vague ones (is this a good answer), and why you give the judge the evidence, not only the response.

The cheap trick that matters: ask for the reasoning first and the verdict second, then convert to structured output as a separate step (Instacart describes decoupling the two so constrained decoding does not hurt the judgement). Use low temperature and, for high-stakes criteria, multiple votes.

In finance the judge is part of a control environment. A compliance reviewer will ask: what does the judge check, how do you know it is right, who reviews its disagreements. So record the judge prompt version, the model version, the human agreement rate by criterion, and keep a human sampling process for the highest risk categories. Never let an LLM judge be the only thing standing between a generated answer and a customer on a regulated topic; for that you want a deterministic check or a human-approved content library.

topics.title: Why offline green does not mean online good
topics.brief: Golden sets are written by you, from yesterday's traffic, in clean text. Production brings distribution shift, new products, noisy speech, angry users and adversarial users. So online evaluation (shadow mode, canaries, A/B tests, sampled human review) is part of the harness, and its findings flow back into the offline set.
practice: Shadow mode: the new model or prompt runs on live traffic and its output is logged but never shown. You compare its intent, confidence, answer and tool calls against the live system and review the disagreements. It costs tokens but carries no customer risk.
Canary: ship to 1 to 5 percent of traffic or one segment, with automatic rollback on guardrail metrics (fallback rate, handoff rate, complaint flags, latency, judge scores on sampled traffic).

A/B test on outcome metrics: containment (resolved without a human), CSAT, repeat contact within 7 days, and cost per conversation. Intercom frames automation rate as involvement rate times resolution rate, which separates how often the bot gets a chance from how well it does with it.
Interleaving is more common in search and ranking; for assistants the analogue is offline pairwise preference on sampled shadow outputs, which needs far fewer samples than a full A/B test.

Human review sampling: random sample for unbiased quality, plus targeted samples (low confidence, thumbs down, handoffs, long conversations, regulated topics). LinkedIn built tooling to evaluate on the order of 500 conversations a day for hallucination and responsible AI issues.

Close the loop: each reviewed failure is labelled, becomes a golden-set row, and often a new intent, a new guardrail or a content fix. Langfuse describes this as a loop where online catches the edge cases the dataset missed.
say: I'd never promote on offline numbers alone. I'd run the candidate in shadow, look at where it disagrees with production, then canary it behind guardrail metrics, and feed whatever we find back into the golden set.
topics.deep:
The offline set has three structural blind spots. First, selection: it contains what you thought to include, so unknown unknowns are absent. Second, time: language and products change, and a model trained or tuned on last quarter's phrasing meets this quarter's. Third, channel: text tests do not reproduce ASR errors, interruptions or silence on a call, so a voice assistant needs its own audio-level tests and its own online monitoring.

Outcome metrics also need care. Containment can go up because the bot got better, or because it made it harder to reach a human, which is exactly the doom loop the CFPB warns about. So pair containment with a quality signal that cannot be gamed by trapping users: repeat contact, complaint rate, abandonment after fallback, and human-reviewed resolution. Klarna's 25 percent drop in repeat inquiries is a better signal than raw chat share, though critics note it does not say how it was measured or how case mix was controlled.

In a regulated setting, experimentation itself needs governance. You usually cannot A/B test a new compliance answer on customers the way you test a button colour, so new content for regulated topics goes through approval first and the experiment covers routing and presentation. Be ready to say which parts of the assistant you will experiment on freely and which you will only change through a controlled release.

topics.title: What to log per turn, and what you must not keep
topics.brief: You cannot do error analysis on logs you did not write. The useful record is per turn and structured: the utterance, the predicted intent with confidence and top alternatives, slots, flow state, latency by stage, tokens, tool calls and results, handoff reason and an outcome label. In finance every field has a PII and retention decision attached.
practice: Per-turn record: conversation id, turn index, channel, utterance (redacted), ASR confidence for voice, intent, confidence and top-k, extracted slots, flow or dialogue state, policy decision, retrieved document ids with scores, prompt and model version, tool calls with arguments and results, guardrail verdicts, per-stage latency, input and output tokens, response, handoff reason, and an outcome label at conversation end.

Use OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions where you can: a span per model call named by operation and model, with gen_ai.operation.name, provider, model and gen_ai.usage.input_tokens and output_tokens, plus execute_tool spans and invoke_agent spans in one trace tree. The conventions were still marked in development status, so pin a version.
OTel keeps prompts and completions as opt-in events instead of span attributes, which is a privacy-friendly design: keep sensitive text out of indexed fields and out of default capture.

Trace tools sit on top: Langfuse (open source, datasets, online judges on sampled traces), LangSmith, Arize Phoenix (OpenTelemetry-based). In regulated finance the deciding factor is often self-hosting or VPC deployment, not features.

Redact before storage: detect and mask account numbers, SSNs, card numbers, names and addresses. Microsoft Presidio is an example, with redact, replace, hash and encrypt operators, and it documents that it cannot guarantee it finds all PII, so you layer controls.

Retention is a policy decision with legal input. FINRA Regulatory Notice 24-09 says recordkeeping rules apply to AI-generated and AI-assisted records and that standard chatbot responses to specific inquiries may be retail communications, so the stored record of what the bot said is itself something compliance may need to retrieve.
say: I'd log every turn as a structured trace with the intent, confidence, top alternatives, tool calls and latency per stage, redact PII at the edge before it lands in analytics, and treat the raw transcript as a regulated record with its own retention and access rules.
topics.deep:
Two stores usually end up existing. An observability store, with short retention, redacted text and wide access for engineers, used to debug and evaluate. And a system of record for conversations, with long retention, access controls and audit logging, used for compliance, complaints and discovery. Mixing them is the common mistake: either engineers get access to raw customer data they should not see, or the compliance record is thin because the debug store rotates.

Redaction has a cost. Aggressive masking removes exactly the tokens (amounts, dates, product names) that error analysis needs, so teams replace values with typed placeholders (an account number becomes a typed token, an amount stays as a bucket) to keep structure. Test redaction on real-looking data with recall measured, because a missed SSN in a log is an incident.

Do not forget decision provenance. For every answer you want to reconstruct why it was given: which prompt and model version, which content version was retrieved, which tool result was used. In a complaint or exam, the question is not just what the bot said but what source of truth it relied on at that moment. Versioning the approved-content library and logging the version id on each answer makes that answerable.

topics.title: Dashboards and alerts that find real problems
topics.brief: Latency and error rate are not enough for an assistant. The signals that catch real breakage are behavioural: fallback and handoff rate by intent, confidence drift, repeat contact, and cost per conversation. Alerts should be on changes from a baseline, per intent and per release.
practice: Quality signals: fallback rate, no-match rate, clarification rate, handoff rate by reason, thumbs down, abandonment right after a bot turn, and repeat contact within a window. A spike in fallback after a release usually means a regression or a new phrasing, such as a marketing campaign that changed what people ask.

Model signals: average and distribution of top-1 confidence, share of utterances below threshold, drift in the intent mix. A shifting intent mix is often a business event (outage, fee change, market move) and a useful early warning for the business too.

Latency by stage and by percentile: p50 hides pain, so alert on p95 and p99 for each stage (ASR, NLU or router, retrieval, LLM first token, tool calls, TTS). Time to first token is a headline metric for streaming.

Cost signals: tokens in and out per conversation, cost per conversation and per resolved conversation, cache hit rate, share of traffic reaching the large model. OTel's token usage metrics, including cache variants, let you build this without a separate billing pipeline.
Safety signals: guardrail trips, blocked outputs, detected PII in outputs, prompt-injection detections, and any answer on a regulated topic that did not come from the approved library.
Judge scores on a sampled slice (5 to 10 percent is a common starting point) trended over time, with human spot checks. Alert on a drop of a set size over a window, not on single scores.
say: I'd alert on behaviour per intent, not just uptime: fallback and handoff rates against a baseline, confidence drift, p95 per stage and cost per resolved conversation, and I'd slice every one of those by release so a regression points at a deploy.
topics.deep:
Slice before you aggregate. A global fallback rate of 8 percent can hide an intent whose fallback rate went from 2 to 40 percent while others improved. Dashboards need cuts by intent, channel (chat vs voice), customer segment, release version and prompt version, because the cause of a spike is almost always one of those.

Alert fatigue is real. Use baselines that account for time of day and day of week, set thresholds on relative change with a minimum volume, and route different alerts to different owners: a latency alert to the platform team, a fallback spike to conversation designers, a safety trip to risk. Every alert should link to the traces behind it, so the first action is reading ten conversations, not guessing.

In finance add an incident path. A wrong answer about fees, rates or eligibility is a potential compliance issue, so there should be a defined process: contain (switch the topic to a fixed fallback or a human), assess how many customers saw it (this is where complete per-turn logs pay off), correct, and record. The ability to kill a single flow or topic with a feature flag, without a deploy, is worth building early.

topics.title: Cost levers: cascade, route, cache, shorten
topics.brief: Most conversational traffic is a small set of easy intents, so the large model should be the exception, not the default. The levers are a cascade (cheap classifier or embedding router first, LLM only when needed), smaller models for narrow jobs, caching, shorter prompts, and fine-tuning only when it clearly pays.
practice: Cascade: an embedding or small classifier model handles high-confidence known intents, and only low-confidence or open-ended turns reach an LLM. FrugalGPT reports matching the best single model with up to 98 percent cost reduction by cascading, and notes model prices differ by up to two orders of magnitude.

Learned routers: RouteLLM trained routers on human preference data and reported over 85 percent cost reduction on MT-Bench at 95 percent of GPT-4 quality, sending only 14 percent of queries to the strong model. The gains were smaller on other benchmarks (45 percent on MMLU), so measure on your own traffic.
DoorDash's guardrail is a cascade too: a cheap semantic-similarity check first, and an LLM evaluator only when the first tier flags a problem.

Prompt caching: cached input tokens cost roughly a tenth of normal input on Anthropic (writes cost a premium), and cut latency on long prompts. Put the stable part (system prompt, policy, tool definitions) first and the variable part last.

Response and retrieval caching: cache answers to identical or near-identical FAQ questions keyed on normalised text or an embedding, with a TTL and invalidation tied to content version. Never cache anything personalised or account-specific.

Shorten context: summarise old turns, retrieve fewer and better chunks, trim tool output before it enters the prompt. Input tokens dominate cost on long conversations, and they also inflate time to first token.

Fine-tune when you have a narrow, stable task with lots of labelled data (intent classification, extraction, routing) or need a small model to match a large one on one job. Do not fine-tune to inject facts that change; use retrieval for those.
say: I'd start the other way round from most demos: handle the common intents with a cheap classifier or embedding router, use the LLM only for what needs it, cache the stable prompt prefix, and measure quality per intent after each cost cut so a saving is not a hidden regression.
topics.deep:
A cascade only saves money if the router is well calibrated. If it sends too much to the cheap path you lose quality silently; too little and you save nothing. So you tune the confidence threshold on a labelled set, look at the cost and error trade-off curve, and monitor the share of traffic at each tier. The cheap path also needs its own failure handling: when the classifier is confident and wrong, nothing downstream catches it, which is why high-risk intents get a stricter threshold or a confirmation step regardless of confidence.

Batching helps on the offline side (judge runs, embeddings of the corpus, nightly evaluation) where latency does not matter, and most providers discount batch work. It does not help the live path, where you want streaming and low time to first token instead.

Be wary of two false savings. First, a small model that needs three retries and more guardrail calls can cost more than one call to a larger model. Second, token cost is often not the biggest line: human handoff cost, QA review, compliance review and platform fees can dominate, so optimise the whole cost per resolved conversation and not just the tokens. In finance, one more constraint: the model and any caching layer must sit inside the approved data boundary, which can rule out a cheap option on contractual grounds before you ever compare prices.

topics.title: Voice latency is a budget you spend per stage
topics.brief: On a phone call people notice a pause after about a second, so the whole pipeline (endpointing, ASR, intent or LLM, tools, TTS, network) has to fit a budget. Most of the delay is turn-taking and LLM time to first token, which is why streaming and a fast routing tier matter more than a bigger model.
practice: A typical budget quoted for production voice agents: endpointing 150 to 300 ms, final ASR 100 to 200 ms, LLM time to first token 300 to 600 ms, TTS time to first byte 100 to 250 ms, network and telephony 50 to 150 ms, for roughly 0.8 to 1.5 seconds total. Treat these as ranges to measure against, not guarantees.
Stream everything: partial transcripts into the prompt builder, tokens into TTS at the first sentence boundary. If a stage waits for the previous one to finish you lose the budget.
Measure percentiles, not averages. p50 can be fine while p95 is a long silence, and callers remember the silences.
Use a fast path for simple intents: a classifier or embedding router answers a balance or hours question with a templated response without any LLM call, saving the largest chunk of the budget.

Cover tool latency: an API call to a core banking system can cost more than the LLM. Use filler or acknowledgement phrases, run independent calls in parallel, and set timeouts with a graceful fallback.
Trim context: long history inflates time to first token every turn, so summarise earlier turns and keep the stable prefix cached.
say: For voice I'd write the latency budget per stage first, stream end to end, route the simple intents around the LLM, and watch p95 per stage in production, because the pauses callers hate live in the tail.
topics.deep:
Turn-taking is the least glamorous and most important piece. If endpointing waits too long you add dead air; if it cuts in too early the assistant talks over the customer. Both feel broken, and the right setting depends on the caller (a person reading out a long account number pauses mid-number). Teams tune endpointing per prompt type, for example longer patience when collecting digits, and support barge-in so the caller can interrupt.

Speech-to-speech models promise to remove stages and cut time to first audio sharply, but in a regulated setting they have trade-offs: less control over exactly what is said, harder transcripts for the record, and harder insertion of deterministic steps like confirmation and disclosures. A cascaded pipeline gives you a text checkpoint where you can apply guardrails, redact, log and require an approved phrasing, which is why many financial deployments stay with it.

Budgets interact with accuracy. A faster, smaller ASR or LLM saves milliseconds and may add errors on account numbers or amounts, so the evaluation harness for voice should include audio test sets with noise and accents and measure error on the high-stakes tokens, not just overall word error rate.

topics.title: Cost per resolved conversation, not calls deflected
topics.brief: Deflection counts conversations the bot did not escalate. Resolution counts conversations where the problem was actually solved. Optimising deflection can push cost down while customers give up, call back, or complain. The metric to defend is cost per resolved conversation, checked against repeat contact and complaints.
practice: Intercom separates deflection (the AI answered, the customer may have left unsatisfied) from resolution (issue addressed and the customer confirmed or did not come back with the same question), and warns vendors often count non-escalated chats as resolved. Fin's automation rate is involvement rate times resolution rate.

Klarna reported 2.3 million chats in the first month, two-thirds of chats, work equal to 700 agents, resolution in under 2 minutes against 11, a 25 percent drop in repeat inquiries and about 40 million dollars of estimated 2024 profit improvement. In 2025 it began rehiring humans for complex cases, a reminder that the numbers depend on case mix and on quality holding.

The Pragmatic Engineer's reading of Klarna: mostly level-one questions, unclear how repeat inquiries were measured, and selection effects, since simple cases go to the bot. Quote the numbers with that caveat.

Full cost counts platform fees, engineering, content upkeep, QA and compliance review, not just tokens. Intercom's guide on evaluating vendors asks for total cost of ownership and identical-data bake-offs.

Content hygiene moves resolution more than model choice in many cases. A vendor-reported study says 2 to 4 weeks of knowledge base cleanup before launch gave about 12 points higher resolution; treat that as vendor data, but the direction matches what teams report.

Regulators care about the failure side: the CFPB lists doom loops, failure to recognise a consumer invoking rights, and inaccurate information, and expects meaningful access to a human for disputes and complex problems.
say: I'd report cost per resolved conversation alongside repeat contact and complaint rate, because deflection can look great while customers are just giving up. And I'd make sure the handoff to a human is easy for anything touching money or disputes.
topics.deep:
The number that executives want is savings, and the number that regulators and customers care about is outcome. The honest way to hold both is a funnel: conversations started, conversations where the bot was involved, conversations resolved without a human (confirmed by no repeat contact within some window), conversations handed off with context, and the cost of each bucket. Then cost per resolved conversation falls out, and you can see whether it fell because resolution rose or because the denominator got small.

Handoff quality is part of cost. A handoff that passes the transcript, the detected intent, the verified identity and the attempted actions saves the human agent minutes and reduces customer repetition. A blind handoff gives you the worst of both: you paid for the bot turn and you pay again, with an annoyed customer.

In financial services the asymmetry matters. A deflected balance question that was answered correctly is cheap and fine. A deflected dispute or hardship request is a possible compliance failure, so many firms define protected intents that always route to a human or a deterministic flow with a human option, and exclude them from the containment target. Saying that out loud shows you think about the metric as something that shapes behaviour.

themes.blurb: Which classifier when, thresholds and out-of-scope, and embeddings as infrastructure.

topics.title: Choosing the classifier: encoder, SetFit, embeddings, or an LLM
topics.brief: There is no best intent classifier, only a best fit for your label volume, label stability and latency budget. Fine-tuned encoders win on stable, high-volume, latency-bound traffic. LLMs and few-shot methods win when labels are scarce or change weekly. Most production systems end up as a cascade, not a single model.
practice: Fine-tuned encoder (BERT, DistilBERT, DeBERTa, or Rasa's DIET for joint intent and entities): cheapest per call, best with hundreds of examples per intent. One small comparison found BERT-base about 20x faster than a 2B-parameter LLM (277 vs 12 samples per second).

Embeddings plus logistic regression or kNN: the cheapest strong baseline. Casanueva et al. showed dual sentence encoders (USE, ConveRT) beat full BERT-Large fine-tuning on BANKING77 at 10 or 30 examples per intent, trained in minutes on one CPU.

SetFit (Hugging Face, Intel Labs, UKP): contrastive fine-tune of a sentence transformer on a few pairs, then a small classification head. About 8 examples per class, roughly 30 seconds of V100 training, and it works multilingually with a multilingual backbone.

LLM zero or few-shot: no training data, handles label churn and gives a rationale, but it is slow and costly per call. Studies agree it wins in few-shot settings and tends to lose to fine-tuned BERT-style models when you have full data.

Cascade: a cheap model scores every request and only uncertain ones escalate to an LLM. A 2025 ACL industry paper does this for out-of-scope detection on CLINC150 and BANKING77, so the LLM sees only the ambiguous slice.
Start order I would use: embeddings plus logistic regression as a baseline, then SetFit or an encoder when you have data, and an LLM as the escalation tier and as a labeling aid.
say: I don't pick the model first. I pick by how many labeled examples per intent we have, how often the intent list changes, and the latency budget, then I start with an embedding plus logistic regression baseline so everything else has to beat something real.

In a bank I'd lean on a cascade: a small fast classifier handles the confident bulk, and only the uncertain slice goes to an LLM, which keeps cost and latency down and keeps the LLM away from most traffic.
topics.deep:
The honest framing is a three-way trade: data, change rate, and cost per request. With almost no data, an LLM prompt or SetFit gets you running in days. With thousands of labeled utterances and a stable taxonomy, a fine-tuned encoder is usually more accurate on the closed set, far cheaper, and deterministic, which matters for audit. The LLM has two durable jobs even when an encoder is in front: handling the long tail of ambiguous requests, and bootstrapping labels for new intents.

The cascade only works if the first stage is well calibrated, because its confidence decides who escalates. The uncertainty-driven routing paper lists this as its main limitation: miscalibration degrades the filter and thresholds still need tuning per deployment. So the cascade and the calibration topic below are one design, not two.

In regulated finance, determinism and explainability favour the small model for anything that triggers an action, and an LLM output used to route to an action should be constrained to the closed intent list and validated. The LLM can also be a rater, not a router: use it offline to label a backlog, then train the small model on the labels after human review.

topics.title: Confidence, calibration and the reject threshold
topics.brief: A softmax score is not a probability that the answer is right, and modern networks are overconfident. A fixed 0.5 cut-off is arbitrary. You set the threshold per intent risk from a held-out set, and you calibrate first so the number means something.
practice: Guo et al. (2017) showed modern networks are poorly calibrated; temperature scaling, one scalar fit on held-out data, fixes much of it without changing the top-1 prediction or accuracy.
Max softmax probability is the baseline for spotting misclassified and out-of-distribution inputs (Hendrycks and Gimpel), but some OOD inputs still score high, so it is a baseline, not a guarantee.

Vendor defaults differ and are only starting points: Dialogflow CX uses 0.3 as its ML classification threshold, Rasa's FallbackClassifier defaults to 0.7, and Microsoft CLU lets you set a None score threshold per project.

Per-intent thresholds by risk: Microsoft's CLU guidance gives an example of about 0.40 for a greeting but 0.95 for a specific action like placing a call. In banking the same logic puts a transfer well above an FAQ.
Rasa adds an ambiguity check: if the top two intents are within a margin, fall back even when the top score clears the threshold. Margin often catches confusions that a single score misses.
Tune on a held-out set that includes real out-of-scope traffic, plot precision against coverage, and pick the operating point for each action class. Re-tune after any retrain.
say: I treat the raw softmax as a ranking signal, not a probability. I calibrate on held-out data, usually temperature scaling, and then pick thresholds per action risk, so a funds transfer needs a much higher bar than an FAQ.
The threshold is a business decision shown as a precision and coverage curve. I'd show the team what each operating point costs in wrong actions versus clarifying questions and let risk sign off.
topics.deep:
Calibration and thresholding are two different jobs. Calibration makes the score honest, so 0.9 means about 90 percent of such predictions are right. Thresholding decides what to do at each score. Temperature scaling does not change which class is top, so it cannot hurt accuracy, but it can reorder which predictions fall under a threshold. Fit it on a split that was not used for training or threshold tuning, and check expected calibration error before and after.

Calibration drifts. When traffic shifts, for example during a market event or a new product launch, a threshold tuned last quarter may let through more wrong answers. So I would monitor the confidence distribution and the fallback rate as live metrics, and treat a sudden change in either as a signal to investigate, not just a number.

Below-threshold does not have to mean give up. Rasa's two-stage fallback asks the user to confirm the likely intent, then asks them to rephrase, then hands off. Showing the top two candidates as quick replies turns uncertainty into a one-tap disambiguation, which is cheaper than a wrong action and less annoying than a flat fallback. For money movement, a confirmation step is needed anyway, so a medium-confidence intent can be routed to a confirm-first path.

topics.title: Out-of-scope detection and the in-scope trade-off
topics.brief: The costly failure in a bank assistant is not a missed intent, it is a confident wrong one. CLINC150 was built to expose this, and its finding is that tightening out-of-scope detection costs in-scope accuracy. You manage that trade, you do not remove it.
practice: CLINC150 (Larson et al., EMNLP 2019): 150 intents across 10 domains plus out-of-scope queries, about 22,500 in-scope. It showed that models near-perfect on closed-set accuracy still misfire on queries they were never taught about.

The paper reports the trade-off directly: raising the out-of-scope bar catches more out-of-scope queries but misroutes some legitimate ones. Its BERT results were roughly 92.6 percent in-scope accuracy against 86.2 percent out-of-scope recall.

Two ways to handle it: a confidence threshold on the in-scope classifier, or an explicit out-of-scope or None class trained on real negative examples. Microsoft CLU recommends adding near-miss false positives (like 'I want to buy a book' for a flight bot) to the None intent.
Mine negatives from real logs: smalltalk, competitor questions, other-product questions, and adversarial probes. Synthetic negatives alone under-represent what customers actually type.
Evaluate with a metric that separates the two errors: in-scope accuracy, out-of-scope recall, and false-accept rate at a fixed in-scope accuracy, not one blended F1.
BANKING77 (77 fine-grained banking intents, 13,083 queries) is the other benchmark: single domain, so the hard part is confusable neighbours like card arrival versus delivery estimate, not topic.
say: For a bank I'd care more about false accepts than missed intents, because a confident wrong action is the expensive failure. So I measure out-of-scope recall at a fixed in-scope accuracy and train the None class on real near-miss queries from logs.
Closed-set accuracy on something like BANKING77 can look great and tell you nothing about what happens on an off-topic question, which is why CLINC150's out-of-scope split matters.
topics.deep:
Out-of-scope is not one thing. There is out-of-domain (weather question to a banking bot), out-of-scope but in-domain (a real banking question the assistant does not support yet, like a product you do not offer), and in-scope but ambiguous. They need different responses. The first can get a polite redirect. The second should route to a human or to a documented policy answer, and the logs of the second are your product backlog. The third needs a clarifying question.

Threshold-only detection is the common baseline and works reasonably with a calibrated model. Explicit None-class training helps most with the near-miss cases, because those are the ones that score high on a wrong intent. In practice use both: a None class for known confusables and a threshold as a safety net for the unknown.

For regulated use, log every rejection and review a sample on a schedule. The rejected set is where a model is quietly failing, and it is also the evidence a model-risk reviewer will ask for when you claim the assistant stays inside its approved scope.

topics.title: Label noise, imbalance, long tail and labeling budget
topics.brief: In practice the classifier is rarely the bottleneck, the labels are. Even the standard banking benchmark has a lot of suspect labels, and real intent distributions are long-tailed. Fixing the taxonomy and the labels usually beats a bigger model.
practice: Label Errors in BANKING77 (ACL Insights, 2022) found over 1,400 of 10,003 training utterances (about 14 percent) potentially mislabeled, using confident learning and similarity methods. Removing them raised F1 by about 4.5 percent.

Confusable intents are often a taxonomy problem, not a model problem. Microsoft's CLU guidance says to read the confusion matrix and merge intents that are mistaken for each other, or add distinguishing examples.
Annotation guidelines need decision rules and boundary examples per intent pair, an explicit rule for multi-intent utterances, and a measured inter-annotator agreement before you scale labeling.

Long tail: head intents dominate traffic and tail intents have a handful of examples. Options are class reweighting, logit adjustment or balanced softmax, oversampling with paraphrase, and few-shot methods like SetFit for the tail. Track per-intent recall, not only overall accuracy.

Active learning from logs: sample production utterances where the model is uncertain or where top-two margin is small, label those first, and add them to training. Walmart's engineering team wrote about selecting NLU training data from conversation logs this way.
Use an LLM to pre-label and a human to review the disagreements with the current model. That spends the labeling budget where it changes the decision boundary.
say: Before touching the model I'd look at the confusion matrix and a sample of the errors. Usually two intents are really one, or the labels disagree, and fixing that helps more than a model upgrade.
For the long tail I'd report per-intent recall, and spend the labeling budget on uncertain production utterances instead of random samples.
topics.deep:
Label noise sets a ceiling. If 1 in 7 training labels in a well-known benchmark is questionable, then headline accuracy differences of a point or two between models are partly noise. In a company dataset labeled by a vendor team over time, expect worse. Cheap checks: train with cross-validation and list examples where the out-of-fold prediction confidently disagrees with the label, which is what confident-learning tools do, then review those by hand.

Imbalance has two sides. Overall accuracy rewards head intents, but a compliance-relevant intent like a complaint or a fraud report might be rare and important. Weight evaluation by risk, not frequency, and keep a hand-built golden set that covers every intent at least a minimum number of times. Microsoft's tooling flags intents with fewer than 15 labeled instances as under-trained, a useful floor to quote.

Active learning works best as a loop, not a project: score new traffic weekly, pull the uncertain and the new-cluster items, label, retrain, and compare against the frozen golden set so you can see real improvement. Keep the golden set separate from anything used for sampling or threshold tuning, or the numbers will flatter you.

topics.title: Hierarchical, multi-label and multilingual intents
topics.brief: Real utterances often carry two intents, and a flat list of a few hundred intents gets unmanageable. A hierarchy keeps decisions small and auditable, multi-label handles compound requests, and multilingual needs per-language thresholds, not one shared one.
practice: Hierarchy: classify a coarse domain first (cards, payments, accounts, investing), then a fine intent within it. Research on label-hierarchy-aware intent models reports gains from a coarse auxiliary task over flat classification.
Hierarchy helps operations too: owners per domain, fallback at the coarse level when the fine level is unsure ('this looks like a card question'), and a smaller review surface for compliance.

Multi-label: a message like 'freeze my card and tell me my balance' needs sigmoid outputs or a split step, and order matters for the dialogue plan. Plain single-label softmax silently drops one of them.
Multi-intent is often handled by splitting the utterance into clauses first, then classifying each, which reuses a single-label model and keeps thresholds meaningful.

Multilingual: a multilingual sentence-transformer backbone gives cross-lingual transfer (SetFit reports results in German, Japanese, Mandarin, French and Spanish), and CLU has a multilingual project flag. Still hold a per-language golden set, because thresholds calibrate differently per language.
Dialogflow CX sets the ML classification threshold per language per flow, which reflects that one number rarely fits all.
say: I'd keep the taxonomy hierarchical so a wrong fine intent can still fall back to the right domain, and so each domain has an owner and its own review.
For multilingual I'd test per language, because a threshold tuned on English can let through far more wrong answers in another language.
topics.deep:
The flat-versus-hierarchical decision is mostly about operations, not accuracy. A hierarchy lets you route an uncertain fine-grained prediction to a safe coarse behavior, like opening the right menu or the right specialist queue, instead of failing outright. The cost is error propagation: a wrong coarse decision cannot be recovered at the fine level, so give the coarse classifier a conservative threshold and a general-purpose branch.

Multi-label raises evaluation questions too. Exact-match accuracy is harsh; per-label precision and recall are more useful, and you need a rule for whether a compound request is worth supporting or should trigger a clarification like 'Let's do one at a time, which first?'. In a bank that is often the safer design, since each action needs its own confirmation anyway.

For multilingual, pooled training data usually helps low-resource languages, but a shared embedding space does not guarantee equal quality. Build a small evaluation set in each language, ideally written by native speakers and not machine-translated, because translated test sets are easier than real customer text.

topics.title: Choosing and adapting an embedding model
topics.brief: MTEB rank is a weak guide for a finance workload. FinMTEB found general-benchmark rank had a statistically insignificant relationship to finance performance. You pick by testing on your own labeled queries, then weigh dimension, storage and hosting.
practice: Build a small evaluation set from your own traffic (queries with known correct intents or documents) and compare 3 to 4 candidates on it. That beats any leaderboard.

MTEB caveats: models can be trained near its datasets, binary relevance hides ranking quality, and some tasks are saturated. FinMTEB (64 finance datasets, English and Chinese) found general-benchmark rank is a poor predictor of finance results; finance-adapted models like Fin-E5 and voyage-3-large tied near the top.

Dimension and cost: OpenAI text-embedding-3 and Voyage models are Matryoshka-trained, so you can truncate vectors. OpenAI reports a 256-dimension text-embedding-3-large still beats ada-002 at 1536 dimensions on MTEB. Voyage reports int8 at 1024 dimensions within 0.31 percent of float at 2048 with 8x less storage.

Task-specific input types: Cohere Embed v3 requires an input_type (search_document, search_query, classification, clustering) and warns that classification and clustering change vector geometry, so do not mix them with retrieval vectors.

Domain adaptation: fine-tune with contrastive pairs (query and positive passage, with in-batch negatives and mined hard negatives) using Sentence Transformers' MultipleNegativesRankingLoss, optionally with Matryoshka loss. Synthetic query generation from your own documents is the cheap way to get pairs.

Domain-tuned commercial options exist: Voyage publishes voyage-finance-2 among others. Fine-tuning gains of 10 to 30 percent on specialized content are claimed in vendor and practitioner write-ups; treat these as hypotheses to test.
say: I wouldn't pick an embedding model off the MTEB leaderboard. I'd build a small eval set from real queries and test a few candidates, because finance text has boilerplate and jargon that general benchmarks barely test.

If retrieval is weak I'd first try a domain model or a light fine-tune on contrastive pairs from our own documents, and I'd check Matryoshka truncation or int8 to cut index cost before paying for more hardware.
topics.deep:
The decision has four axes: quality on your data, vector size, latency and cost, and where the data is allowed to go. Quality should be measured on recall at k for retrieval and on macro-F1 for classification using vectors, with a held-out set. Vector size drives index memory linearly, so a 3072-dimension float vector is 12 KB each; at tens of millions of vectors that is a real bill, which is why truncation and quantization matter. Always re-evaluate after truncating, since the loss is small on average but can be larger on your hard queries.

Fine-tuning embeddings is worth it when the domain vocabulary or the notion of similarity differs from general web text, for example when 'rollover' means one thing for a 401(k) and another for a CD. It carries a cost: you now own a model, an evaluation set, and a re-embedding job each time you retrain. Try cheaper levers first: query rewriting, a reranker, hybrid lexical plus dense search, and metadata filters.

In a regulated firm, hosted embedding APIs mean sending customer text to a third party. FINRA Regulatory Notice 24-09 says its rules apply whether you build or use a third party's model, and SR 11-7 style model risk expects vendor models to be inventoried and validated. So self-hosting an open model in your own cloud, or a private deployment from a major cloud provider with contractual no-retention terms, is often the path; also redact or tokenize account numbers and personal data before embedding.

topics.title: Semantic routing and cheap first-pass classification
topics.brief: Semantic routing compares the embedding of a request to embedded example utterances per route and picks the closest. It is fast, cheap and deterministic, and it is a good guardrail layer in front of an LLM. It is also a classifier, so it needs the same thresholds and out-of-scope handling.
practice: semantic-router (Aurelio Labs): you define routes with example utterances, embed them, and match a new query by cosine similarity to the nearest utterances, skipping an LLM call for the routing decision.
Typical uses: route to a flow (balance, dispute, transfer), block off-topic or risky topics before the LLM sees them, and select a tool or a specialist agent.
Each route needs a similarity threshold, and below it the query falls to a default route or a clarifier. Tune thresholds per route on held-out real queries, as with any classifier.
Keep the utterance sets curated and versioned: adding a loose example to one route can steal traffic from a neighbour. Test against a frozen regression set on every change.
Use it as stage one of a cascade: confident matches go straight to the deterministic flow, borderline queries go to an LLM or a clarifying question.
Latency is the selling point: one embedding call plus a nearest-neighbour lookup, often tens of milliseconds, versus a full LLM generation.
say: I like semantic routing as a first gate in front of the LLM: it's fast and predictable, and it makes decisions I can audit. But it's still a classifier, so I'd tune per-route thresholds and keep a regression set for the utterance lists.
For anything sensitive, like a transfer, the route only selects the flow. The flow itself is deterministic and asks for confirmation.
topics.deep:
Routing by embedding similarity is nearest-neighbour classification with hand-written exemplars. That makes it easy to explain to a compliance reviewer: here are the example phrases per route, here is the threshold. It also makes failures easy to fix, because you can add or remove an utterance without retraining. The weaknesses are the usual ones: negation ('do not freeze my card'), entity-dependent meaning, and short ambiguous inputs like 'yes' or 'the second one', which depend on dialogue context and should not go through the router in isolation.

Put context handling in front of it: if the assistant just asked a question, interpret the reply in that frame before routing. Otherwise the router will send a bare 'yes' somewhere random.

Embedding-based routing and fine-tuned classifiers are interchangeable at this layer. If you have enough labeled data, a trained classifier on top of the same embeddings usually beats raw nearest-utterance matching, and you can keep the router for new intents that do not have data yet.

topics.title: Intent discovery, clustering and deduplication from logs
topics.brief: You find new intents by clustering real conversations, not by brainstorming in a meeting. Embeddings plus UMAP plus HDBSCAN find the groups, an LLM names them, and a human decides which become intents. HDBSCAN is chosen because it does not need a cluster count and it marks noise.
practice: BERTopic pipeline: sentence embeddings, UMAP dimension reduction, HDBSCAN clustering, then keyword or LLM labels for each topic.

Intercom's Fin team describes their version: extract the key question from each conversation with a small LLM, embed with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, UMAP, HDBSCAN into subtopics, recursive clustering into parent topics, then an LLM to name and tidy.

Intercom assigns new conversations to the nearest cluster centroid and flags anything with similarity below 0.5 as a possible emerging topic. About 10 to 15 percent of conversations land as noise, and centroid assignment cut outliers by about half.
They report clustering algorithm and hyperparameters mattered more than the choice of embedding model, and that cleaning boilerplate, merging fragmented turns and removing spam came first.

Deduplication: near-duplicate utterances inflate head intents and leak between train and test splits. Dedupe by embedding similarity above a tight threshold before splitting, or your accuracy is overstated.
Keep a human in the loop for approving a cluster as an intent; check each cluster for whether one flow can serve all its members, which is the real test of whether it is one intent.
say: To find new intents I'd cluster real logs with embeddings and HDBSCAN, have an LLM propose names, and then have a person decide which clusters deserve to be intents, based on whether one flow would serve them all.
I'd dedupe near-identical utterances before making train and test splits, otherwise the test set leaks and the accuracy looks better than it is.
topics.deep:
Clustering finds similar wording, not similar needs. Two clusters can need the same action, and one cluster can hide two actions. So the review question is operational: can one answer or flow handle every example, and what would the assistant do differently for each cluster? The size and growth of each cluster, and its fallback rate, tell you what to build next.

The noise group deserves attention. HDBSCAN deliberately declines to force outliers into clusters, and the outlier set is where genuinely new or unusual requests live, plus junk. A weekly pass that re-clusters the noise, or compares it to existing centroids, is a cheap emerging-topic detector.

In finance, be careful about what goes into the pipeline. Logs contain account numbers and personal data, so redact before embedding or labeling with a hosted LLM, keep retention rules, and note that analyzing logs can itself fall under data-use agreements. Research on unsupervised intent induction for customer support dialogue is a useful reference for the broader approach, though I could not read the full paper text here.
