topics.title: Embedding drift, re-embedding cost and index choices
topics.brief: Embeddings are a dependency with a version. Changing the model changes the vector space, so the whole index must be rebuilt, and live traffic drifts away from your reference set over time. Plan the migration and the monitoring before you need them.
practice: Vectors from different models are not comparable even when dimensions match, so you cannot mix them in one index. Safe migration: add the new vector as a second column or index, backfill while the old one serves, compare recall on a golden set, then cut over atomically.

Cost is a line item: one source estimates re-embedding a large corpus at roughly 166 dollars with OpenAI text-embedding-3-small and about 1,079 dollars with 3-large for its example corpus, and larger corpora need hours of GPU time if self-hosted.
Research like Drift-Adapter proposes a small learned mapping from old to new space for near zero-downtime upgrades; treat it as a research idea, not a default.

Drift monitoring: compare reference and current embedding batches. Evidently tested five methods (Euclidean and cosine on centroids, a domain classifier, share of drifted components, MMD) and recommends the classifier-based ROC AUC score as a stable default.
Practical signals: rolling centroid distance against a 30-day baseline, share of queries below the cluster-similarity floor, fallback rate, and the fraction of queries landing in the noise cluster.

Index choices briefly: pgvector is fine to a few million vectors and keeps data in your database; dedicated engines (Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, OpenSearch) add scale and filtering; HNSW is the usual in-memory graph index and IVF with quantization trades recall for memory.
say: I treat the embedding model like a pinned dependency. If we change it, we re-embed into a parallel index, check recall on a frozen golden set, and only then cut over.
For drift I'd watch the embedding distribution of live queries against a reference window and the fallback rate, and a jump in either triggers review of the taxonomy and the thresholds.
topics.deep:
Two kinds of drift get confused. Input drift is the world changing: new products, a market event, a new fee policy, so queries cluster differently. Model drift is you changing the model: an API provider deprecating a version, or your own retrain. The first shows up in the monitors above. The second is prevented by pinning versions and using deprecation notices as a calendar item. A hosted embedding model that is silently updated would invalidate the stored vectors and every threshold tuned against them, so prefer providers with versioned model names and a deprecation policy.

A classifier-based drift test, training a model to tell last month's embeddings from this month's, gives an AUC that is easy to explain and alert on: near 0.5 means no meaningful shift. Centroid distance is cheaper but can hide shape changes. Whatever you choose, tie the alert to an action, like sampling and labeling the drifted slice.

On indexes, the quality knob that matters more than the engine is the evaluation set. Measure recall at k against exact search on your data, then pick the cheapest index and quantization that holds it, and pair with metadata filters for things like product line or entitlement so a user only retrieves content they are allowed to see.

topics.title: Financial-domain specifics: FinBERT, BANKING77 and regulated data
topics.brief: Finance text is full of boilerplate and jargon, so domain models help, but FinBERT is a sentiment model, not an intent classifier. The bigger constraint is governance: customer text, third-party hosted models and model-risk rules shape what you can use more than accuracy does.
practice: FinBERT (Araci, Prosus) is BERT further trained on financial text and fine-tuned on Financial PhraseBank for three-way sentiment. Useful as a domain-adapted backbone idea, but not a drop-in intent model.

FinMTEB reports FinBERT beating BERT by about 15.6 percent on finance embedding tasks, and finance-adapted embeddings like Fin-E5 doing better than their general bases, so domain adaptation pays off here.

BANKING77 is useful for practice because intents like card payment fee charged versus transfer fee charged are close neighbours, which mirrors real banking confusions. It is a public customer-service-style dataset, not your traffic, so do not assume its accuracy transfers.

A 2023 study on banking text classification with limited resources compared LLM prompting, retrieval-augmented prompting and fine-tuned models on banking data; I could not read the full text, so check its numbers before quoting.

FINRA Regulatory Notice 24-09 says existing rules apply to gen AI, including when a firm uses a third party's tool, and points to model risk management, data privacy and accuracy. SR 11-7 style guidance treats vendor foundation models as third-party components to be validated.

Data handling: redact or tokenize account numbers, SSNs and names before sending text to any hosted model; prefer private deployments with contractual no-training and no-retention; keep an inventory of every model and version used for classification.
say: In finance I think the governance questions come first: where does customer text go, which vendor model version is it, and who validated it. Then I pick the simplest model that meets accuracy, and a small self-hosted classifier often fits that better than an external API.
I'd use a benchmark like BANKING77 to practise on confusable banking intents, but I'd never trust its numbers for our own traffic.
topics.deep:
Domain models are one lever, but in a bank the usual wins come from process: a cleaned and agreed intent taxonomy, a golden test set covering every intent and every risk class, and per-intent thresholds that risk has approved. Those artifacts are also what a model-risk reviewer wants: documented purpose, data lineage, validation results, ongoing monitoring and a change-control record.

Hosted LLMs and embedding APIs are not forbidden, but they are third-party components. Under FINRA 24-09 and SR 11-7 style expectations the firm stays responsible for outputs and has to evaluate the tool before use. That is a good reason to keep the first-pass classifier small and in-house, use hosted LLMs behind redaction for the ambiguous slice, and log inputs, model versions and decisions so you can reconstruct why a request was routed the way it was.

As a caveat on my research: I could not confirm vendor-specific data residency terms here, and those change often. For an interview, say that you would check each vendor's current data-use and retention terms with the firm's security and legal teams, instead of quoting terms from memory.

topics.title: Voice assistants: where the errors and the milliseconds go
topics.brief: A voice assistant is a chain, and the errors multiply: a 95% accurate ASR feeding a 98% accurate NLU gives about 93% end to end. Word error rate is the wrong number to chase on its own. What matters is the error on the words that carry meaning (digits, names, tickers, dollar amounts), and how the dialogue recovers when those are wrong.
practice: Treat ASR and NLU as one system: train or evaluate intent models on ASR output (real transcripts with errors), not only clean typed text. Passing the n-best list or confidence instead of only the 1-best transcript gives the NLU a way to hedge.

Bias the recogniser toward the domain: custom vocabulary or phrase hints for fund names, tickers and product names, and grammar-style constraints for digit strings. Measure entity-level accuracy per slot, not just WER.

Endpointing decides when the user has finished. Too eager cuts people off, too slow feels dead. Published tuning guidance puts about 250 ms of silence for purposeful IVR-style callers and about 400 ms where people think aloud, and the better systems add a linguistic signal (is the sentence complete) on top of silence.

Barge-in has two layers: the media layer stops outbound audio on detected speech, and the logic layer cancels the pending LLM call, synthesis and tool calls. The metric is time from the interrupting syllable to agent silence. Echo cancellation matters or the bot interrupts itself.

Latency budget for a cascaded pipeline, one published example: about 80 ms endpointing, 120 ms ASR, 180 ms LLM, 70 ms TTS for sub-500 ms perceived. Human turn gaps are around 200 ms. For slow tool calls, emit a short real acknowledgement tied to actual system state, never a fake filler.

Read back and confirm what is costly to get wrong: digit strings in chunks, spelled names with the NATO alphabet as a fallback, amounts and dates. Offer DTMF (keypad entry) as the deterministic fallback for account numbers and PINs after one or two failed attempts.
say: I think about a voice bot as a chain where each stage's errors multiply, so I would measure slot-level accuracy on the words that matter, like numbers and names, instead of staring at overall word error rate.
The way I'd do it is confirm only what is expensive to get wrong, and give the caller a keypad fallback after a couple of misses rather than looping on recognition.
topics.deep:
The classic IVR to conversational IVR migration is less about the model and more about the design contract. Directed-dialogue IVRs ask one question, constrain the grammar, and are very accurate on narrow input. Conversational IVRs open the first prompt ('how can I help?') and route on natural language, which raises containment on the long tail but exposes you to ASR errors on open vocabulary. The usual production pattern is hybrid: open prompt for intent, then tightly constrained collection for the identifiers, with DTMF always available. Teams measure intent accuracy on real call audio, and compare against the old menu's misroute rate before turning anything over.

With LLMs the pieces change shape but the failure modes remain. A speech-to-text front end can still mangle a ticker or an account number, and an LLM will happily make a fluent guess out of a wrong transcript. So the confirmation step and the deterministic collection of identifiers stay outside the model. Some teams use native speech-to-speech models for natural prosody and turn-taking, but in regulated settings many keep the cascaded design because you can log and audit the transcript at each stage and gate what the TTS says.

What I would stress in a finance interview: audio is a regulated record (calls are often recorded, and redaction of card or account numbers in transcripts is a requirement), noisy mobile calls and older callers are the segments where WER is worst, and an accent or dialect gap is a fairness issue you can measure by slicing error rate by cohort. A good answer names the metric (entity accuracy, barge-in latency, time to first audio, containment, escalation rate) and the fallback (DTMF, human).

topics.title: Human handoff and agent assist: containment is not the goal
topics.brief: The mistake is optimising containment (the share of conversations the bot finishes) as if every escalation were a failure. A good handoff is a feature: the right case reaches a person fast, with the transcript, the identified customer and the intent already attached, so the customer never repeats themselves. Regulators have specifically named the bot that cannot hand off.
practice: Define escalation triggers explicitly: the customer asks for a person (always honour it), two or three consecutive fallbacks or repeated rephrases, low confidence on a high-stakes intent, negative sentiment or rising frustration, a complaint or dispute, vulnerable-customer cues, and any intent the policy marks human-only.

Warm transfer carries context: authenticated identity, intents seen, slots collected, a short summary and the last few turns. Dialogflow CX exposes a LiveAgentHandoff signal with custom metadata, and platforms such as Twilio Flex and NICE pass the transcript to the desktop.

Agent assist is the same stack pointed at the human: knowledge suggestions, suggested replies, live summarisation, sentiment, and after-call summaries (Google's Agent Assist lists these). Many firms start here, because a human stays between the model and the customer.

Close the loop: the human agent's corrections, dispositions and the escalated transcripts are the best labelled data you have. Mine escalations for missing intents and broken flows, and feed approved answers back into the knowledge base.

Measure handoff quality, not only rate: repeat-contact rate within 7 days, transfer-to-resolution time, how often the agent re-asks identification, and customer satisfaction split by bot-only versus handed-off.
say: I wouldn't treat every escalation as a failure. I'd track whether the handoff arrives with context, because the real damage is the customer having to repeat everything to the agent.
The escalations are the most useful data we have, so I'd read a sample every week and turn the patterns into new intents, fixes, or knowledge articles.
topics.deep:
Frustration detection is easy to oversell. Sentiment models trained on general text are noisy on short utterances ('no' and 'agent' and 'representative' repeated), and in voice, anger is better caught by the behaviour (repeated reprompts, barge-in on every prompt, silence, repeated 0 key presses) than by a score. The robust production rule is a combination: a hard rule for explicit requests and repeated failure, plus a softer model signal that raises priority rather than deciding alone.

When to escalate is also a risk decision. In finance some intents should never be fully automated: complaints, disputes, hardship, bereavement, suspected fraud, and anything that sounds like personalised advice. Those are routed on detection of the topic, not after the bot has tried. The business design question is what the bot is allowed to attempt before it gives up, and the answer should come from compliance as well as from containment targets.

The CFPB has described bots that trap customers in loops with no route to a person and has said it expects firms to ensure a path to human service. That makes the escalation path a compliance control, not a nice-to-have. Agent assist adds its own risks: the human may over-trust a suggested reply, so approved-content links and visible sources matter, and an AI-written case summary becomes a record that may need retention.

topics.title: Authentication and personalisation: what the assistant may say before and after login
topics.brief: Identification (who do you claim to be) is not verification (prove it), and an assistant needs a policy for each intent on what is allowed unauthenticated, after light authentication, and only after step-up. Personalisation without authentication is a data leak waiting to happen, and voice biometrics alone is no longer treated as safe because cloned voices exist.
practice: Tier the intents by data sensitivity. Unauthenticated: public FAQs, fund information, branch hours. Authenticated session: balances, positions, statements. Step-up: money movement, changing contact details or bank links, anything that is irreversible.

In a logged-in app the session already carries authentication, so the assistant inherits it and the token scopes limit what tools can be called. On a phone line, authentication happens inside the conversation, so the flow collects an identifier, then a knowledge, possession or biometric factor, then caches the result with an expiry.

Step-up means re-challenging for risky actions (a one-time code to a registered device, an in-app approval) even inside an authenticated session. Risk signals such as new device, odd hour, a just-changed phone number or a large amount raise the bar.

Voice biometrics: low friction and good against a human impostor, but vulnerable to cloning from a few seconds of audio, replay and relay attacks. Industry write-ups describe banks rethinking voice as a sole factor and pairing it with liveness or deepfake detection, device signals and a risk decision.

Keep sensitive values out of the model's reach until needed: the LLM sees only what the tool returns for that authenticated user, never a broad customer record, and logs redact account numbers. Do not let a spoken name or last four digits alone unlock anything beyond public content.
say: I'd design it per intent: what is public, what needs a logged-in session, and what needs a fresh challenge, and I'd keep the model from ever seeing data the current user hasn't earned.
I wouldn't rely on a voiceprint alone. It's a good signal in a risk decision, not a lock.
topics.deep:
For an LLM assistant the most important auth property is that the authorisation lives in the tool layer, not in the prompt. A prompt that says 'only show balances to verified users' is advice; a balance tool that rejects a call without a verified session scoped to that customer is a control. This also defends against prompt injection and a user asking the assistant for another person's account. Each tool call should carry the authenticated principal, and the policy check should be deterministic code.

Personalisation in finance is regulated by what it implies. Saying 'your balance is X' is retrieval. Saying 'you should move money into this fund' based on the client's holdings is personalised advice, which carries suitability and fiduciary obligations. Vanguard's own CIO has publicly said the assistant must not cross into unauthorised financial advice, which tells you where the line is drawn. A common design is to let the assistant explain, summarise and retrieve, while recommendations come from an approved advice engine or a human advisor.

Privacy details interviewers like: consent and purpose limitation for using account data in prompts, data residency and vendor retention terms for the model provider, masking in transcripts, and retention schedules for chat and voice logs. A good answer shows you would ask these on day one.

topics.title: The LLM agent era: who owns the flow, the model or the code
topics.brief: Every enterprise platform now splits the work between an LLM and deterministic flows, and they draw the line in different places. The useful question is per intent: does the model decide what to do next (planner), or does it only interpret the user while a fixed flow runs the transaction (flow)? In regulated finance the answer for money and account actions is almost always the flow.
practice: Rasa CALM: the LLM does dialogue understanding only, turning the user's message into commands such as start a flow or set a slot. Business logic lives in explicit flows that call APIs and branch deterministically. The model never improvises the steps of a transfer.

Dialogflow CX: classic visual state-machine flows (predictable and easy to audit) plus generative playbooks, where you describe behaviour in natural language and Gemini plans tool calls. Teams mix them: a playbook for open conversation, a flow for the sensitive path.

Copilot Studio: topics (authored flows) plus generative orchestration, where the model chooses among topics, tools and knowledge sources, with generative answers behind confidence checks. Rasa's own comparison argues the deterministic boundary is less explicit there than per turn in CALM (a vendor view, take it as one).
Kore.ai XO (Mphasis's main partner): combines dialog tasks with GenAI features. I have only the vendor positioning, so describe the split as a design choice rather than claiming product specifics.

Production patterns that hold across them: a router or orchestrator picks a lane (FAQ with retrieval, API lookup, transactional flow, human); tools have typed schemas and server-side authorisation; every tool call is logged with arguments; a hard step or turn budget stops runaway loops; sensitive actions require a confirmation step the model cannot skip.
say: I'd let the model interpret and the code decide for anything that moves money or touches an account. The model proposes a command, a deterministic flow validates it and does the work.
For open questions I'm happy to give the model more freedom, as long as it is grounded in retrieved content and every tool call is logged so we can replay a bad turn.
topics.deep:
The trade-off is coverage against control. A flow-first design is predictable, testable and easy for compliance to read, but every new capability costs authoring effort and the bot sounds rigid. A planner-first design covers the long tail with little authoring, but it is harder to test (non-deterministic paths), harder to explain to an auditor, and prone to wrong tool choice or skipped confirmation steps. Most banks end up with a layered system: deterministic for transactions and compliance statements, retrieval-grounded generation for FAQs, and a planner only where the action space is read-only and low risk.

Evaluating an agent is different from evaluating a classifier. You test trajectories, not just answers: did it choose the right tool, with the right arguments, in the right order, and did it stop and ask when it should. Teams build scenario suites from real transcripts, replay them on every prompt or model change, and track tool-call accuracy, task success, escalation correctness and policy violations. The model version and the prompt are part of the release, so changes go through regression like code.

Vanguard's public job postings for AI application engineers mention agentic architectures on AWS Bedrock with LangGraph, MCP and tools for models from several providers, evaluation and monitoring for responsible AI, and a conversational AI orchestration platform. That matches the orchestrator pattern above, and it is worth asking how they split flows from agents.

topics.title: Model risk management for LLM assistants in a bank
topics.brief: Banks run models under supervisory model risk guidance: inventory, independent validation, ongoing monitoring, documentation. The old US guidance, SR 11-7, applied to LLMs by principle, but reporting from April 2026 says it was replaced by a new letter, SR 26-2, which excludes generative AI from scope. Practising banks keep validating anyway, because separate GenAI guidance is expected and the risk has not gone away.
practice: Treat the LLM system as one thing under validation: the foundation model version, system prompt, retrieval configuration, tools and guardrails are versioned together, with an owner and a risk tier in the model inventory.

Validate on in-domain data: a test set built from real queries, measuring groundedness (is each claim supported by a source), hallucination rate against a threshold, refusal correctness, and robustness to adversarial prompts. Generic leaderboards are not evidence.

Independent challenge: someone who did not build it reviews conceptual soundness, limits and test results. For third-party models, assume the provider can change behaviour without notice, so pin versions and re-run the suite on every change.

Explainability for LLMs usually means traceability: the answer cites its sources, the tool calls and the prompt version are logged, and a reviewer can replay a decision. Do not claim the model's internal reasoning is explainable.

Bias and fairness: slice quality and escalation rates by cohort (language, accent for voice, channel), and watch for different refusal or tone patterns. Audit logs record who asked, what the model saw, what it answered and what the human did next.
Compensating controls that regulators and reviewers like: human in the loop on risky outputs, approved prompt libraries, content filters, and a kill switch.
say: I treat the prompt, the model version, the retrieval setup and the tools as one versioned system, and I re-run the evaluation suite on any change to any of them, because a silent model update can change behaviour.
For explainability I'd focus on traceability: every answer links to its source and every tool call is logged, so a reviewer can replay the turn.
topics.deep:
Generative AI breaks three assumptions in classic model validation: outputs are not deterministic, there is no fixed specification to validate against, and the core model is usually built by someone else. The practical response is to move validation from the model to the system and the process: a defined scope of use, an evaluation set with agreed pass thresholds, sampling of live conversations, and monitoring for drift in inputs, retrieval quality and refusal patterns.

On the regulatory status, be careful in an interview. A trade-press report (Risk.net) says US regulators replaced SR 11-7 with SR 26-2 on 17 April 2026 and excluded GenAI from its scope, while noting that large banks kept validating GenAI and that separate guidance is expected. I could not confirm the text of SR 26-2 myself, so say 'as I understand it' and show you know the principle either way: independent validation, monitoring and effective challenge.

Around the model sit conduct rules. FINRA's Regulatory Notice 24-09 (June 2024) says existing rules apply to generative AI: supervision (including model risk and data integrity), communications rules where a chatbot reaches customers, recordkeeping of AI-generated content, and data protection. Vanguard's public statements describe monitoring for model performance, bias and drift, and compliance and legal buy-in, which is the shape an interviewer will expect.

topics.title: What regulators have said about financial chatbots
topics.brief: Regulators do not have a special chatbot rulebook: existing consumer protection and conduct rules apply to whatever answers the customer. The two public anchors are the CFPB's 2023 chatbot report (the doom loop, wrong answers, no route to a human) and FINRA's 2024 notice on generative AI (supervision, communications, recordkeeping).
practice: CFPB issue spotlight on chatbots in consumer finance (June 2023): flags noncompliance risk, harm from wrong or inconsistent information, erosion of trust, and doom loops where the customer repeats the same exchange with no offramp to a person.
Design response: an always-available human option, a cap on repeated fallbacks before escalation, and clear disclosure that the customer is talking to an automated assistant.

FINRA Regulatory Notice 24-09 (27 June 2024): no new rules, but existing rules apply: a supervisory system that covers GenAI, communications rules depending on audience, retention of AI-generated records, and protection of customer data.

In practice this means logging every conversation with the model and prompt version, retaining it on the required schedule, reviewing a sample for compliance, and keeping approved language for regulated content (performance, fees, risks).

Hallucination in this setting is a conduct problem, not only a quality problem: a wrong fee or a wrong tax statement is a misstatement to a customer. Vanguard's own investor research found 37% of AI users received wrong or misleading information.
say: I'd treat the bot's answers like any other customer communication, so they get logged, retained and sampled for review, and anything regulated comes from approved content rather than being generated.
I'd make sure there is always a way out to a person, because a bot that can't hand off is the exact failure the CFPB called out.
topics.deep:
The retrieval-versus-generation split is where compliance and engineering meet. Statements about performance, fees, risk or eligibility are the ones regulators examine most closely, so a common design serves them from a compliance-approved library, with the model choosing which approved item applies rather than writing new text. Open-ended explanatory content can be generated, but only from approved sources and with a refusal when the evidence is missing.

Communications rules also raise a quiet question: is a chatbot answer an individual correspondence, retail communication or something else? FINRA's notice says it depends on the nature and number of recipients. That affects whether pre-approval or post-review applies, and a candidate who knows the question exists sounds experienced.

One caution: these are US sources and Vanguard is a US firm, but Vanguard also operates under SEC rules for investment advisers, and its Personal Advisor and Digital Advisor services are advisory products. Anything that edges toward a recommendation changes the regulatory frame, which is why public statements from its CIO stress staying clear of unauthorised advice.

topics.title: What Vanguard has said publicly about its AI and assistants
topics.brief: Vanguard's public line is augment, do not replace: AI as an enabler that amplifies human expertise. The concrete items are Crew Assist for contact-centre staff on Azure OpenAI, GenAI client-ready article summaries for advisors, an internal chatbot piloted with about 2,000 employees on questions like account balance, and a CIO who has talked about a client-facing digital advisor and even a voicebot. Use this to ask informed questions, not to claim inside knowledge.
practice: Crew Assist: one of the first Azure OpenAI uses, where contact-centre staff ask a question and get an answer drawn from internal content, with links to share. The aims are faster resolution, better answer quality and quicker onboarding. This is retrieval-grounded agent assist, the safest first step.

Client-ready article summaries (announced May 2025, beta): advisors generate customised summaries of Vanguard's market perspectives by client sophistication, life stage and tone, with the required disclosures generated alongside. Reported reach is about 150,000 advisors across 50,000 advisory firms.

Internal chatbot pilot: about 2,000 employees testing natural-language answers to client-style questions such as account balance and portfolio performance. The CIO has stressed watching hallucinations and keeping it from giving financial advice, and has talked of a digital advisor for roughly 50 million clients.

Governance as reported by MIT Sloan Management Review: monitoring for performance, bias and drift, tracking of crew AI usage, a few dozen pilots with most unreleased, about $500 million of AI value tracked across cost avoidance, shareholder value, risk reduction and efficiency.

Partners named publicly: WRITER as the enterprise generative AI platform and Norm AI for compliance, plus Azure OpenAI. Public job postings add AWS Bedrock, LangGraph, MCP, Python, TypeScript, Splunk and Honeycomb, with a team that owns conversational AI orchestration platforms and shared AI infrastructure.

Vanguard's own investor research found about a third of its investors had used AI for financial guidance, 37% of those had received incorrect or misleading information, and only a few percent of investors highly trust AI guidance compared with more than half for human advisors. Expect that to shape a cautious, human-in-the-loop design.
say: From what Vanguard has said publicly, the pattern is augment first, with Crew Assist for the contact centre and advisor tools, then careful client-facing steps. I'd expect grounding, monitoring and a human path to matter more than clever generation.
I'd be curious how you split the deterministic account lookups from the generated explanations in the client assistant, since the pilot questions include balances and performance.
topics.deep:
What I could not find: any public detail on how Vanguard's current client virtual assistant is built (vendor, NLU stack, intent counts), its containment numbers, or its voice channel design. The interviewers may mention things I could not verify, so listen first. The sensible inference from the public record is a layered setup: retrieval-grounded content assistants for staff and advisors, an authenticated client assistant that reads from account APIs, and orchestration code on a cloud agent framework.

The job postings are the best public window into the team. The orchestration-platform role asks for experience with agent orchestration, conversational AI, agent-to-agent protocols, RAG, knowledge management and semantic search. The application engineer role asks for agentic chat on AWS Bedrock with LangGraph, system prompts, skills and tools for models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, evaluation and monitoring, and Python or TypeScript. For a conversational AI and NLP contractor role through Mphasis, expect work close to that stack: intent and entity design on an existing assistant, error analysis on transcripts, classification and embedding work for routing and retrieval, and LLM components under guardrails.

A good move in the interview is to connect your own experience to their stated priorities: evaluation harnesses, production monitoring, grounding by source type, and safe escalation. Do not name their internal systems as if you knew them.

topics.title: Mphasis and conversational AI: the integrator's view
topics.brief: Mphasis is a systems integrator, not a model lab. Its conversational AI practice is built around a Next Gen Contact Center offering and a partnership with Kore.ai, where it describes itself as the only platinum professional services partner. As a contractor placed through them, you are expected to deliver on the client's stack, so show you adapt to platforms and care about measurable outcomes.
practice: Public positioning: Mphasis.ai business unit for generative AI, Next Gen Contact Center combining conversational and generative AI, analytics and automation, aimed at banking, financial services and insurance, healthcare, retail and travel.

Kore.ai platform (per the partnership press): a no-code and pro-code platform for virtual assistants across 40+ channels and 120+ languages, with Kore.ai claiming service to over 200 Global 2000 companies. I have only press claims here.

Mphasis describes multi-algorithm intent engines that combine machine learning, knowledge graphs and industry ontologies, human-in-the-loop escalation (simple account questions to bots, advisory matters to specialists), and agentic AI for context-aware decisions.

Claimed results in its own blog, all vendor numbers and unverified: 25% faster resolution, 10 to 15% better first-call resolution, 30% cost savings. Treat them as marketing, and talk about how you would measure such outcomes instead.
Its stated guardrails: hallucination mitigation by fine-tuning and letting the model say it does not know, AES-256 encryption, compliance with SOC 2 and ISO 27001, and bias detection.
say: I don't tie myself to one platform. What carries over is intent and entity design, error analysis on real transcripts, evaluation and safe escalation, and I pick up the vendor's tooling quickly.
I'd want to know which stack the Vanguard team runs, and where my work would sit: new intents, classifier quality, retrieval, or the LLM layer.
topics.deep:
In an integrator arrangement the engineer's value is speed to useful work inside someone else's system. That means reading existing assistants (intent taxonomy, training data quality, fallback analysis), proposing changes that can be measured, and documenting them so the client team can own them after you leave. Interviewers from the client side will probe for judgement more than for platform trivia.

The one thing I could not find was any public statement that Mphasis builds Vanguard's virtual assistant. The only public Mphasis conversational AI partner I found is Kore.ai. Do not assume Vanguard runs Kore.ai, and do not say so. Ask what platform and models the team uses today.
